title: Everything That Has Breath
subtitle: Psalms 107–150 in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
Book Five of the Psalter is the last and fullest: songs of the redeemed, the great alphabet psalm about God's word, the fifteen Songs of Ascent the pilgrims sang on the road to Jerusalem, a lament by the rivers of Babylon, and a closing crescendo where everything that has breath is told to praise.

This volume answers them one at a time, forty-four short poems in five parts, each beside a picture and under a single line from the psalm it answers. It completes the four-volume Psalms in Poems & Pictures.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Keep the Psalms open alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

paintings.title: say so
paintings.epigraph: “He makes the storm a calm, so that its waves are still.”
paintings.poem:
four stories of people in trouble:
lost in the desert,
chained in the dark,
sick almost to death,
tossed on the sea.

and four times, the same line:
they cried to the Lord,
and he saved them.

he stilled the storm
and brought them
to the harbor they longed for.

if he's rescued you—
say so.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “say so” (Psalm 107:23–30)—where the poem notes, “if he's rescued you— say so”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: borrowed words
paintings.epigraph: “My heart is steadfast, God. I will sing and I will make music with my soul.”
paintings.poem:
this psalm is stitched together
from two older ones—

old prayers,
reused
for a new day.

nothing wrong with that.

my heart is steady.
I'll sing.

sometimes you borrow
yesterday's words
until today's
catch up.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “borrowed words” (Psalm 108:1–5)—where the poem notes, “until today's catch up”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: wounded
paintings.epigraph: “for I am poor and needy. My heart is wounded within me.”
paintings.poem:
this psalm is full of curses—
raw, angry,
the words of a man
repaid evil for love.

the Bible doesn't clean them up.

but notice where he takes them:
not to revenge.
to God.

I am poor and needy.
my heart is wounded.
help me.

bring the anger
to the only One
who can hold it
and judge rightly.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “wounded” (Psalm 109:21–26)—where the poem notes, “who can hold it and judge rightly”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: my Lord
paintings.epigraph: “Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand”
paintings.poem:
one of the most quoted psalms
in the New Testament.

the Lord says to my Lord:
sit at my right hand.

David calling someone
greater than himself
Lord.

Jesus asked the scholars
who that could be.

they didn't answer.
we know.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “my Lord” (Psalm 110:1–4)—where the poem notes, “they didn't answer. we know”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: pondered
paintings.epigraph: “Yahweh’s works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them.”
paintings.poem:
his works are great—

studied,
pondered,
by everyone who delights in them.

the stars,
the seasons,
the life of a friend—

wonder
is its own kind
of worship.

and the beginning of wisdom?
awe.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “pondered” (Psalm 111:2–10)—where the poem notes, “and the beginning of wisdom? awe”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: bad news
paintings.epigraph: “He will not be afraid of evil news. His heart is steadfast, trusting in Yahweh.”
paintings.poem:
bad news is coming.
it always is.

a messenger.
a letter.
a knock.

and the righteous
aren't afraid—

not because they're sure
the news will be good,
but because their hearts
are fixed
on the One who isn't surprised.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in Psalm 112:7?

paintings.title: stoops so low
paintings.epigraph: “He raises up the poor out of the dust. Lifts up the needy from the ash heap”
paintings.poem:
who is like the Lord,
who sits so high
and stoops so low?

he lifts the poor from the dust,
the needy from the ash heap,

and seats them
with princes.

and the woman who couldn't have children—
a home full of them.

the higher he is,
the lower he bends.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “stoops so low” (Psalm 113:5–9)—where the poem notes, “the higher he is, the lower he bends”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: flint
paintings.epigraph: “who turned the rock into a pool of water, the flint into a spring of waters.”
paintings.poem:
when Israel came out of Egypt,
the sea looked and ran.
the Jordan turned back.
the mountains skipped like rams.

tremble, earth,
before the God
who turns flint
into a spring.

nothing is too hard
to become water
in his hands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “flint” (Psalm 114:1–8)—where the poem notes, “to become water in his hands”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: not to us
paintings.epigraph: “Not to us, Yahweh, not to us, but to your name give glory”
paintings.poem:
not to us.
not to us.

the idols have mouths
but can't speak,
eyes but can't see,
ears but can't hear.

and those who make them,
the psalm warns,
become like them.

we become
what we worship.

so give the glory
to the One
who sees and hears and speaks.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “not to us” (Psalm 115:1–8)—where the poem notes, “to the One who sees and hears and speaks”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: because he listened
paintings.epigraph: “I love Y ahweh, because he listens to my voice”
paintings.poem:
I love the Lord
because he listened.

that's the whole reason,
and it's enough.

and then:
what can I give back
for all his goodness?

the answer is almost funny:
I'll take the cup of salvation.
I'll call on his name.

you repay a giver
by receiving more.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Psalm 116:1–13 (“you repay a giver by receiving more”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: two verses
paintings.epigraph: “Praise Yahweh, all you nations! Extol him, all you peoples!”
paintings.poem:
the shortest chapter
in the Bible.

two verses.

all you nations, praise him.
his love is great.
his faithfulness lasts forever.

some of the longest truths
fit
in the shortest sentences.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “two verses” (Psalm 117:1–2)—where the poem notes, “fit in the shortest sentences”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the cornerstone
paintings.epigraph: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.”
paintings.poem:
the builders looked at it
and tossed it aside.
wrong shape.
not useful.

and it became
the cornerstone,
the stone
the whole building leans on.

Jesus quoted this
about himself.

and then the line
you can say
any morning:

this is the day
the Lord has made.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were to set down one stone of remembrance today for how God has helped you thus far (Psalm 118:22–24), what would you name it?

paintings.title: come find me
paintings.epigraph: “I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant”
paintings.poem:
the longest psalm.
a hundred seventy-six verses,
twenty-two sections,
one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet,

every line
in love with God's word.

a lamp for my feet.
a light for my path.

and after all that devotion,
the very last line:

I've gone astray
like a lost sheep.
come find me.

even the one who loved the law most
ended
needing to be found.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “come find me” (Psalm 119:105–176)—where the poem notes, “ended needing to be found”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: far from home
paintings.epigraph: “In my distress, I cried to Y ahweh. He answered me.”
paintings.poem:
the first Song of Ascent—
songs the pilgrims sang
on the road up to Jerusalem.

it starts far from home,
among people who want war
when I want peace.

every journey toward God
starts
somewhere you don't belong.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “far from home” (Psalm 120:1–7)—where the poem notes, “starts somewhere you don't belong”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the hills
paintings.epigraph: “I will lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from?”
paintings.poem:
the pilgrims looked up
at the hills ahead—
steep,
unknown,
where danger could be waiting.

where does my help come from?

not the hills.
the One who made them.

he won't let your foot slip.
he doesn't doze.
he doesn't sleep.

your going out,
your coming in,
now
and forever.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Psalm 121:1–8 (“now and forever”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: glad
paintings.epigraph: “I was glad when they said to me, “Let’s go to Yahweh’s house!””
paintings.poem:
I was glad when they said:
let's go.

not dragged.
invited.

and then—
our feet are standing
inside your gates.

pray for the peace
of the city.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “glad” (Psalm 122:1–6)—where the poem notes, “pray for the peace of the city”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: eyes on the hand
paintings.epigraph: “as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master”
paintings.poem:
a servant in a busy house
watches the master's hand—
a small gesture,
and he knows what to do.

so our eyes
are on your hand.

not on the crowd.
not on the ones who mock.

on you,
until you show mercy.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “eyes on the hand” (Psalm 123:1–2)—where the poem notes, “on you, until you show mercy”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the snare is broken
paintings.epigraph: “Our soul has escaped like a bird out of the fowler’s snare.”
paintings.poem:
if the Lord hadn't been on our side—
say it, Israel—

the flood would have swept us away.

but look:
the snare is broken,
and we flew out.

we didn't pick the lock.
he broke the trap.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the snare is broken” (Psalm 124:1–8)—where the poem notes, “we didn't pick the lock. he broke the trap”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: surrounded
paintings.epigraph: “As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so Yahweh surrounds his people”
paintings.poem:
Jerusalem sits
with mountains all around her.

that's you,
the psalm says—
surrounded.

not by enemies.
by God.

on every side.
forever.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “surrounded” (Psalm 125:1–2)—where the poem notes, “on every side. forever”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: sow in tears
paintings.epigraph: “He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.”
paintings.poem:
when God brought us home,
it felt like a dream.
we laughed.
we sang.

and for the times
it's not a dream yet:

those who sow in tears
will reap in joy.

the tears
water the seed.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “sow in tears” (Psalm 126:1–6)—where the poem notes, “the tears water the seed”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: go to bed
paintings.epigraph: “for he gives sleep to his loved ones.”
paintings.poem:
unless the Lord builds the house,
the builders work for nothing.

you can get up early.
stay up late.
eat the bread of anxious work.

or you can rest.

he gives
to his beloved
in their sleep.

the house is his project.
you're allowed
to go to bed.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “go to bed” (Psalm 127:1–2)—where the poem notes, “you're allowed to go to bed”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: olive shoots
paintings.epigraph: “your children like olive plants around your table.”
paintings.poem:
children
like olive shoots
around the table.

not finished trees.
shoots—
small,
tender,
needing years.

the psalm isn't promising
a perfect family.
it's describing
a slow, green blessing.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “olive shoots” (Psalm 128:1–3)—where the poem notes, “it's describing a slow, green blessing”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: long furrows
paintings.epigraph: “The plowers plowed on my back. They made their furrows long.”
paintings.poem:
they plowed on my back.
long furrows.

since I was young,
Israel says,
they've afflicted me.

but they haven't won.

the Lord is righteous.
he cut the cords.

the scars are real.
so is the freedom.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “long furrows” (Psalm 129:1–4)—where the poem notes, “the scars are real. so is the freedom”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the watchman
paintings.epigraph: “My soul longs for the Lord more than watchmen long for the morning”
paintings.poem:
out of the depths
I cry to you.

if you kept a record of sins,
who could stand?

but with you
there is forgiveness.

and so I wait—
more than the night watchman
waits for dawn.
more than the night watchman
waits for dawn.

the repetition is his.
some waiting
you have to say twice.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Psalm 130:1–6 (“some waiting you have to say twice”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: content
paintings.epigraph: “like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.”
paintings.poem:
three verses.
no big questions.

my heart isn't proud.
I don't chase things
too great for me.

I've calmed my soul,
like a weaned child
with his mother—

not crying for milk anymore.
just content
to be close.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “content” (Psalm 131:1–3)—where the poem notes, “just content to be close”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: making room
paintings.epigraph: “until I find out a place for Y ahweh, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob.”
paintings.poem:
David vowed
he wouldn't sleep
until he found a place
for God to live.

and God answered
with a better promise:
I'll establish your house.

we keep trying
to make room for him.
he keeps
making room for us.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “making room” (Psalm 132:1–12)—where the poem notes, “he keeps making room for us”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: running downhill
paintings.epigraph: “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!”
paintings.poem:
how good
and pleasant it is
when brothers live in unity—

like precious oil
running down Aaron's beard,
like the dew of Hermon
falling on Zion's hills.

unity
isn't everyone agreeing.
it's blessing
running downhill
from one to another.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “running downhill” (Psalm 133:1–3)—where the poem notes, “running downhill from one to another”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the night shift
paintings.epigraph: “Lift up your hands in the sanctuary. Praise Y ahweh!”
paintings.poem:
the last Song of Ascent—
for the servants
who stand in the house
by night.

the night shift.
the ones who keep the lamps lit
while everyone sleeps.

lift your hands.
bless the Lord.

he sees
who's worshiping
at three in the morning.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the night shift” (Psalm 134:1–2)—where the poem notes, “who's worshiping at three in the morning”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the weather is his
paintings.epigraph: “He brings the wind out of his treasuries.”
paintings.poem:
clouds rising at the edge of the world.
lightning with the rain.
wind brought out
of his storehouses.

the weather
is not an accident.
it's his.

and the idols?
silver and gold,
made by hands.
no breath in their mouths.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the weather is his” (Psalm 135:5–17)—where the poem notes, “made by hands. no breath in their mouths”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: forever
paintings.epigraph: “Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good; for his loving kindness endures forever.”
paintings.poem:
twenty-six times,
the same answer:
his love endures forever.

creation—
his love endures forever.
the sea parted—
his love endures forever.
he remembered us when we were low—
his love endures forever.

you could read it as repetition.

or you could read it
as a congregation
refusing to stop saying it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “forever” (Psalm 136:1–26)—where the poem notes, “as a congregation refusing to stop saying it”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the willows
paintings.epigraph: “How can we sing Y ahweh’s song in a foreign land?”
paintings.poem:
by the rivers of Babylon
we sat and wept.

we hung our harps
in the willows.

they asked for a song.
how could we?

this psalm ends in words
so bitter
they're hard to read aloud.

they're in the Bible
because grief like this
is real,
and God
wants it brought to him
instead of buried.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the willows” (Psalm 137:1–4)—where the poem notes, “wants it brought to him instead of buried”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: still on the loom
paintings.epigraph: “Y ahweh will fulfill that which concerns me.”
paintings.poem:
the Lord will finish
what concerns me.

what he started,
he completes—
Philippians says it too.

don't abandon
the work of your hands.

I'm the work,
and I'm still
on the loom.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where is God inviting you to set down your work today and rest in what He has already finished (Psalm 138:8)?

paintings.title: wonderfully made
paintings.epigraph: “I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.”
paintings.poem:
where could I go
from your Spirit?

heaven—you're there.
the depths—you're there.
the far side of the sea—
your hand still holds me.
the dark
is not dark to you.

you knit me together
before anyone knew my name.

I am fearfully,
wonderfully made.

and then, the bravest part:
search me.
know me.
lead me.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in Psalm 139:7–14?

paintings.title: the advocate
paintings.epigraph: “I know that Y ahweh will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and justice for the needy.”
paintings.poem:
the violent plot.
the slanderers hiss.

and against all that,
one thing I know:

the Lord takes up
the case
of the afflicted.

the poor
have an advocate
who never loses.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the advocate” (Psalm 140:1–12)—where the poem notes, “have an advocate who never loses”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the door of my lips
paintings.epigraph: “Set a watch, Y ahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.”
paintings.poem:
let my prayer rise
like incense,
my lifted hands
like the evening offering.

and one more request,
maybe the harder one:

set a guard
at my mouth.
keep watch
at the door of my lips.

some prayers are for rescue.
some
are for restraint.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you pause at the threshold of “the door of my lips” (Psalm 141:2–3), what closed place in your life is waiting for you to open to His presence?

paintings.title: no one
paintings.epigraph: “Look on my right, and see; for there is no one who is concerned for me.”
paintings.poem:
written in a cave.

look to my right—
no one.
no one cares for my soul.

sometimes that's how it feels,
and the Bible lets it be said.

and then:
you are my refuge.
my portion
in the land of the living.

the loneliest moment
becomes the place
he's all I have—
and enough.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “no one” (Psalm 142:4–5)—where the poem notes, “he's all I have— and enough”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: in the morning
paintings.epigraph: “Cause me to hear your loving kindness in the morning, for I trust in you.”
paintings.poem:
I spread out my hands to you,
thirsty like dry ground.

let the morning
bring me word
of your unfailing love.

and teach me
the way to walk,

because I've lifted my soul
to you
and have nowhere else
to set it down.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What single step right in front of you is already lit by His word today, even if the far horizon remains unseen (Psalm 143:6–10)?

paintings.title: a breath
paintings.epigraph: “Man is like a breath. His days are like a shadow that passes away.”
paintings.poem:
Lord, what is man,
that you notice him?

a breath.
a shadow passing.

and yet—
you train my hands.
you're my fortress.
you're my loving God.

the breath
is held
by the One who breathed it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a breath” (Psalm 144:1–4)—where the poem notes, “is held by the One who breathed it”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: tell the next one
paintings.epigraph: “One generation will commend your works to another”
paintings.poem:
one generation
tells the next.

grandparents to grandchildren,
parents at the table,
an old friend to a new believer:

here's what he did.

and the Lord is near
to everyone who calls—
every generation,
every voice.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “tell the next one” (Psalm 145:4–18)—where the poem notes, “every generation, every voice”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: princes
paintings.epigraph: “Don’t put your trust in princes, in a son of man in whom there is no help.”
paintings.poem:
don't put your trust
in princes.

their breath goes out.
their plans die with them.

trust the One who
keeps faith forever,
feeds the hungry,
sets prisoners free,
watches over the foreigner,
lifts up the widow and the orphan.

that's the kind of king
worth trusting.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “princes” (Psalm 146:3–9)—where the poem notes, “that's the kind of king worth trusting”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: names and bandages
paintings.epigraph: “He heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds.”
paintings.poem:
he counts the stars
and calls each one by name.

and in the same breath:
he heals the brokenhearted
and binds up their wounds.

the God who names the stars
kneels
with a bandage.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “names and bandages” (Psalm 147:3–4)—where the poem notes, “kneels with a bandage”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: everyone has a part
paintings.epigraph: “Praise him, sun and moon! Praise him, all you shining stars!”
paintings.poem:
sun and moon.
shining stars.
sea creatures and ocean depths.
fire and hail, snow and mist.
mountains and fruit trees.
wild animals and cattle,
creeping things and flying birds.
kings and all peoples,
young and old together.

everything
has a part
in the song.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “everyone has a part” (Psalm 148:1–13)—where the poem notes, “has a part in the song”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: needs your feet
paintings.epigraph: “Let them praise his name in the dance!”
paintings.poem:
praise him
with dancing.
with tambourine and harp.

the Lord takes pleasure
in his people.

he delights in you—
so dance.

some worship is quiet.

paintings.title: if you're breathing
paintings.epigraph: “Let everything that has breath praise Yah!”
paintings.poem:
trumpets.
harp and lyre.
tambourine and dancing.
strings and pipe.
loud cymbals.
crashing cymbals.

and then the last line
of the whole book of Psalms:

let everything that has breath
praise the Lord.

if you're breathing,
you're invited.

praise the Lord.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “if you're breathing” (Psalm 150:1–6)—where the poem notes, “praise the Lord”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?
